n: These psalms of David share a common theme. They reflect on the experience of evil. In {{Psalm 51:1-19|Psalm 51}}, the psalmist admits his wrongdoing and asks for God's forgiveness. {{Psalm 52:1-64:10|Psalms 52–64}} express sorrow over specific evils David faced. A song of praise ({{Psalm 65:1-13|Psalm 65}}) brings David's laments to an end.
The psalmist asks God to protect him and guide him into his presence ({{Psalm 61:4-5|Psalm 61:4–5}}). He prays for God to extend and protect the king's rule and promises to praise God.
In these royal prayers, the psalmist longs for God’s presence. All three psalms concern themselves with the king’s security.

- *the ends of the earth*: This phrase suggests a cry that comes from a place far away from God. 

- The psalmist feels deep sorrow and distress.

- The poet desires God's presence and seeks entry into God's earthly home for protection and care. Being welcomed into God's sanctuary (*tent*) is the greatest blessing (see {{Psalm 15:1|Psalms 15:1}}; {{Psalm 23:6|23:6}}; {{Psalm 24:3-6|24:3–6}}). The Hebrew word for *tent *refers to the tabernacle and the tent David built for the ark ({{1 Chronicles 15:1|1 Chronicles 15:1}}). See also study note on John 1:14. 

- The shelter of your wings represents God's protection and care (see {{Psalm 9:9|Psalms 9:9}}; {{Psalm 17:8|17:8}}).

- *You have heard my vows*: The psalmist's vows might be part of ceremonial sacrifices ({{Psalm 66:13-15|Psalms 66:13–15}}; {{Psalm 76:11|76:11}}; {{Psalm 116:14|116:14}}, {{Psalm 116:18|18}}). He praises and thanks God for rescuing him. 

- The inheritance refers to the promise of the land (see {{Psalm 60:1-12|Psalm 60}}), the sacredness of the temple, the joy of God's presence ({{Psalm 119:111|Psalm 119:111}}), or any similar reward ({{Psalm 16:6|Psalms 16:6}}; {{Psalm 37:9|37:9}}, {{Psalm 37:11|11}}, {{Psalm 37:18|18}}, {{Psalm 37:22|22}}, {{Psalm 37:29|29}}, {{Psalm 37:34|34}}; {{Psalm 127:3|127:3}}).
See {{1 Chronicles 25:1|1 Chronicles 25:1}}; also in {{Psalm 39:1-13|Psalms 39}} and {{Psalm 77:1-20|77}}.

This psalm expresses trust in the king and includes a prayer for him. The king relies on God even during tough times. 

His tricky and strong enemies challenge him, but he stays strong. He urges himself and his people to trust God. 

He wants them to view their human enemies from God's perspective, where they seem weak, temporary, and deceitful ({{Psalm 62:9|Psalm 62:9}}).
The enemies want to overthrow the king using lies and tricks.
*his lofty perch:* This means the royal throne.
The psalmist encourages himself and others to place their hope in God.
*are but a lie*: People often try to appear stronger and better than they truly are.
Humans are temporary, unlike God. Even when successful, their prosperity does not last long.
*Extortion* involves using threats to force someone to give up their belongings. *Stealing* means taking what belongs to someone else.
Only God balances power and loving devotion. He cares for his people by removing those who do evil from the world (see {{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}).

- Together, *soul* and *body* refer to a person's entire being. 

- *dry and weary land*: When David lived in the desert, he felt spiritually empty, away from God's people and the sanctuary.

The king deeply desires God's presence. He experiences God's goodness in everything he does. Despite being tired and troubled by the wicked, the king finds strength in God and praises him. God is his source of life ({{Psalm 63:3|Psalm 63:3}}), while the wicked face destruction ({{Psalm 63:9|63:9}}).
The psalmist remembers that he had found God to be present in his sanctuary (see {{Psalm 18:6|Psalm 18:6}}; {{Psalm 61:4|61:4}}; {{Psalm 62:5|62:5}}, {{Psalm 62:11-12|11–12}}).
*better than life*: The best life comes from a relationship with God (see {{Psalm 4:7|Psalms 4:7}}; {{Psalm 63:5|63:5}}; {{Proverbs 16:8|Proverbs 16:8}}).
Meditating on God requires focus, concentration, thought, and reflection (see {{Psalm 1:2|Psalm 1:2}}).

The psalmist thinks about and feels God's presence during the night. When it is dark, God is the light. The quiet night and the wait for morning offer time to reflect on the true meaning of life with the Lord.

- The wicked planned to ruin the psalmist's life with lies and deceit, but they would fail. 

- *the depths of the earth*: This refers to the place of the dead.

Wild foxes and jackals are often associated with places that are ruined and abandoned ({{Isaiah 13:20-22|Isaiah 13:20–22}}; {{Isaiah 34:10-15|34:10–15}}; {{Jeremiah 9:11|Jeremiah 9:11}}; {{Jeremiah 49:33|49:33}}; {{Jeremiah 51:37|51:37}}; {{Lamentations 5:18|Lamentations 5:18}}; {{Malachi 1:3|Malachi 1:3}}). The wicked will not receive honor in death. Scavenging animals will consume their bodies ({{Ecclesiastes 6:3|Ecclesiastes 6:3}}; {{Jeremiah 22:18-19|Jeremiah 22:18–19}}; {{Jeremiah 36:29-30|36:29–30}}).
These verses form a prayer for rescue from bold and powerful liars.

This lament speaks against the destructive plans and arrogant attitude of the wicked ({{Psalm 64:1-6|Psalm 64:1–6}}). The psalmist prays to God and finds comfort in God's justice because the righteous judge will undo the wicked's actions. The godly will rejoice and gain wisdom as they think about God's powerful deeds.
*their tongues … bitter words*: Liars use their words to harm others. This description might also refer to practicing magic.

- The enemies make a plan to harm the innocent without getting caught. 

- Human beings can act with extreme evil through words, actions, or plans ({{Psalm 83:3|Psalm 83:3}}; see {{Jeremiah 17:9|Jeremiah 17:9}}).
God acts righteously. God stops wickedness and gives the wicked what they intended for others.
God alone deserves praise and is worthy to have vows made to him.
Praise is the right response to God's great acts in redemption ({{Psalm 65:3-5|Psalm 65:3–5}}) and in nature ({{Psalm 65:5-13|65:5–13}}).
This psalm recounts the reasons why all people should praise and revere God for his almighty power and merciful care for his universe.
*You atone*: God graciously removes the guilt of sin (see {{Psalm 32:5|Psalm 32:5}}).

- *the one You choose and bring near*: This includes people from Israel and other nations. 

- Only those God sees as blameless live in his holy courts ({{Psalm 15:1-5|Psalms 15}} and {{Psalm 24:1-10|24}}). 

- At the temple, God's earthly palace, all nations can gather to experience God's holy presence. No structure can separate humans from God (see {{Revelation 21:22|Revelation 21:22}}).

- God brought order to the mountains, the roaring oceans, and the pounding waves (see {{Psalm 95:4-5|Psalms 95:4–5}}; {{Psalm 104:6-9|104:6–9}}). 

- The psalmist compares the chaotic forces of nature with the rebellion of the nations (see {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalms 2:1–12}}; {{Psalm 33:6-11|33:6–11}}; {{Psalm 46:6|46:6}}).
All over the world ({{Job 38:13|Job 38:13}}; see {{Psalm 50:1-3|Psalm 50:1–3}}), people should stand in awe of the Lord.

The *streams of God* and all rivers show God's power and goodness through nature's order and the regularity of the harvests (see {{Psalm 1:3|Psalms 1:3}}; {{Psalm 36:8|36:8}}; {{Psalm 46:4|46:4}}; {{Ezekiel 47:6-12|Ezekiel 47:6–12}}; {{Zechariah 14:8|Zechariah 14:8}}; {{Revelation 22:1|Revelation 22:1}}).
The created world clearly shows God's power ({{Psalm 65:6-8|Psalm 65:6–8}}). He shows his love by taking care of nature. Everything praises the Lord as all parts work together smoothly.
The psalmist urges nature to join a powerful song to praise God's glory, name, and power.
This anonymous psalm includes two hymns ({{Psalm 66:1-12|Psalm 66:1–12}}, {{Psalm 66:13-20|13–20}}) that praise God for saving his people.
The glory of his name represents the perfection of God’s character.

The story of the exodus and God's victory over the sea causes the people to be amazed ({{Psalm 66:5|Psalm 66:5}}) and to worship ({{Psalm 66:6|66:6}}). God performs miracles to redeem people for himself.
God's power brings redemption. The same word appears in {{Psalm 65:6|Psalm 65:6}} to describe God's power in creation (see also {{Psalm 80:2|Psalm 80:2}}).
The orderly lives of the redeemed reflect the order of God’s world. The Lord protects them from evil and purifies them.
God guides his people into wisdom and away from foolishness ({{Psalm 17:5|Psalms 17:5}}; {{Psalm 37:31|37:31}}; {{Psalm 121:3|121:3}}).
*For You, O God, have tested us*: Like a silversmith heats silver to remove impurities, God's discipline removes sin from his people (see {{Psalm 12:6|Psalm 12:6}}).
God decrees and permits the many trying circumstances his people experience.
*You let men ride over our heads*: Or *You made people rule over us.* This likely refers to a foreign ruler who controlled the Israelites.
Vows often included sacrifices of thanksgiving, including burnt offerings (see {{Psalm 20:3|Psalms 20:3}}; {{Psalm 40:6|40:6}}; {{Psalm 50:8|50:8}}; {{Psalm 51:19|51:19}}).
The private testimony at the end of the psalm matches the public praise at the beginning ({{Psalm 66:1-4|Psalm 66:1–4}}).
This prayer is inspired by the priestly blessing in {{Numbers 6:24-26|Numbers 6:24–26}}. God's kindness to Israel influences his reputation among other nations (see {{Psalm 96:1-3|Psalm 96:1–3}}).

This anonymous prayer asks for God's blessing. The psalmist speaks about knowing and worshiping God among all nations (compare {{Psalm 64:9|Psalms 64:9}}; {{Psalm 65:8|65:8}}). The prayer asks for God's name to remain holy and that his kingdom come (compare {{Matthew 6:9-13|Matthew 6:9–13}}).

- God’s international reputation leads to his praise among the nations (see {{Psalm 138:4|Psalm 138:4}}). Their chaos and rebellion will stop when they join Israel in praising God. 

- One God rules over everyone, and the nations will give thanks for God’s just rule (see {{Psalm 67:4|Psalm 67:4}}).
God delivers the ultimate justice that people seek ({{Psalm 96:10|Psalms 96:10}}; {{Psalm 98:9|98:9}}).

- Large harvests show God’s blessing ({{Genesis 26:12|Genesis 26:12}}; {{Isaiah 30:23|Isaiah 30:23}}). 

- *all the ends of the earth*: See {{Psalm 2:8|Psalms 2:8}}; {{Psalm 96:1-3|96:1–3}}. 

- People from every nation will join Israel in acknowledging the God of Israel.
These verses form a prayer for God to rise and scatter his enemies, like when Israel entered the promised land (compare {{Numbers 10:35-36|Numbers 10:35–36}}; {{Joshua 6:1-12:24|Joshua 6–12}}).

This prayer for God's victorious rule describes God's journey from Sinai to Zion ({{Psalm 68:7|Psalm 68:7}}, {{Psalm 68:16-18|16–18}}, {{Psalm 68:24|24}}). He saved Israel from Egypt, led them through the wilderness, brought them to the promised land, and established his kingdom. He is a caring and victorious God, whose nature does not change. Therefore, the faithful hope and rejoice in the promise of God's universal rule.
Both *smoke* and *wax* represent a temporary existence ({{Psalm 22:12-18|Psalms 22:12–18}}; {{Psalm 37:20|37:20}}; {{Psalm 102:3|102:3}}).
The fate of the godly is different from that of the wicked (see {{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}).

*Him who rides on the clouds*: This is an ancient description of Baal, a Canaanite god. The psalmist uses it to describe the Lord as the true God "who rides upon the highest heavens" (see {{Psalm 68:33|Psalms 68:33}}; {{Psalm 104:3|104:3}}). God has power over the clouds and the rain.
The psalmist praises God’s powerful and compassionate reign.

- God, the Father of all marginalized and needy people, shows them compassion and protects their rights (see {{Psalm 10:14|Psalms 10:14}}, {{Psalm 10:18|18}}; {{Psalm 69:33|69:33}}; {{Psalm 82:3|82:3}}). 

- Like his dwelling, the Lord is holy. The supreme example of the holy God coming down to rescue humanity is Jesus Christ.

- God freed Israel from slavery in Egypt ({{Exodus 20:2|Exodus 20:2}}; see {{Psalm 69:33|Psalm 69:33}}), and he continues to free prisoners today. 

- The* sun-scorched land* represents being far from God and separated from blessing.

- The *earth shook* as it does during an earthquake (see {{Exodus 19:18|Exodus 19:18}}). 

- *the heavens poured down rain*: Wells in the desert and rain showers in Canaan provided plenty of water.
*a great company of women proclaim it*: A large group of women singers celebrates the victory in song (see {{Psalm 68:25|Psalm 68:25}}; {{Exodus 15:20|Exodus 15:20}}).
The people who cared for flocks and moved from place to place were surprised to receive silver and gold ornaments from the battle.

- The Almighty (Hebrew *Shaddai*) is an ancient name for God (see {{Psalm 91:1|Psalm 91:1}}; {{Genesis 17:1|Genesis 17:1}}). 

- The exact location of Mount Zalmon is unknown; it might have been a mountain in Bashan (see {{Psalm 68:15|Psalm 68:15}}).

Bashan is a plateau northeast of Jerusalem and east of the Sea of Galilee. It was famous for its forests and pastureland (see {{Psalm 22:12|Psalm 22:12}}; {{Isaiah 2:13|Isaiah 2:13}}). The mountains might have included Mount Hermon to the north of the plateau or Mount Zalmon, possibly Jebel ed-Druze to the east.
*Why do you gaze in envy*: Bashan is more impressive than the mountains around Jerusalem, but it was not the Lord's home. Only Mount Zion had the honor of being God's dwelling place.
Chariots were the top weapon of the military in the psalmist’s time. They represent the Lord’s power to give victory ({{Psalm 20:7|Psalms 20:7}}; {{Psalm 44:3|44:3}}).

- *You have ascended on high*: The Most High victoriously established his reign in Zion. 

- *captives … gifts*: This image shows a victorious ruler leading a victory march after battle. Paul applied this image to Jesus Christ ({{Ephesians 4:8-13|Ephesians 4:8–13}}).
Like a caring father or a shepherd, God carries his people in his arms (see {{Psalm 55:22|Psalm 55:22}}; {{Psalm 68:5-6|68:5–6}}).
God cares for his people like a shepherd, and the people praise him.
*God will crush the heads of His enemies*: Compare {{Genesis 3:15|Genesis 3:15}}.
God will deal with all enemies, whether from high places (represented by *Bashan*) or low (*the depths of the sea*).
A great company joins together in the pilgrimage to Zion.
The people pray for God's help and victory over enemy nations ({{Psalm 68:1-3|Psalm 68:1–3}}).
The conquered kings will bring gifts to the Lord.
Hostile and rebellious people delight in warfare and insurrection (see {{Psalm 2:1-3|Psalm 2:1–3}}).
The phrase *kingdoms of the earth* refers to all nations and power structures.
The psalmist urges the people to praise God, who triumphs over his enemies.
When the Lord shows his power, majesty, and strength to the nations, he makes his people stronger (see {{Psalm 96:4-6|Psalm 96:4–6}}).

{{Psalm 45:1-17|Psalm 45}} also mentions this tune, but {{Psalm 45:1-17|Psalm 45}} praises the glory of kingship. In contrast, {{Psalm 69:1-36|Psalm 69}} is the cry of a tired king who feels abandoned by the Lord.

The psalmist sees himself as almost drowning but still surviving chaotic forces and his sense of separation from God (see {{Psalm 42:7|Psalm 42:7}}; {{Psalm 69:14|69:14}}, {{Psalm 69:15|15}}; {{Isaiah 8:8|Isaiah 8:8}}).
In this personal lament, the poet shares his vulnerability, humiliation, and deep pain. He asks God to defend him for the sake of the righteous.

These last four psalms of Book Two contrast with the earlier psalms that describe God’s mighty acts in creation and redemption, ending with God’s march to Zion ({{Psalm 65:1-68:35|Psalms 65–68}}). {{Psalm 69:1-71:24|Psalms 69–71}} describe the king's suffering, and {{Psalm 72:1-20|Psalm 72}} responds with a prayer for God to bless the king.
John applied this lament to Jesus ({{John 15:25|John 15:25}}).
The psalmist confesses his sins and prays that God’s response to him will encourage others in similar conditions to place their hope in the Lord.
Mistreated and abandoned by family, friends, and community, the psalmist seeks comfort, relief ({{Psalm 69:13-18|Psalm 69:13–18}}), and justice ({{Psalm 69:22-28|69:22–28}}) from the Lord.

The psalmist is devoted to God and what is holy, yet people repay him with insults. Later, this verse was applied to the anger of Jesus at the temple’s money changers ({{John 2:17|John 2:17}}) and his undeserved suffering ({{Romans 15:3|Romans 15:3}}).
When the psalmist denies himself normal comforts to seek God in prayer, the wicked ridicule him.
The psalmist can only pray for rescue and relief from his enemies.
The psalmist feels alone and misunderstood. He cannot bear his doubts, and his troubles overwhelm him.
*vinegar to quench my thirst*: This description applies to the suffering of Jesus ({{Matthew 27:34|Matthew 27:34}}, {{Matthew 27:48|48}}; {{Luke 23:36|Luke 23:36}}; {{John 19:28-29|John 19:28–29}}).
The psalmist asks God to give his suffering ({{Psalm 69:3|Psalm 69:3}}) to his enemies. Paul applied these words to the unbelieving Jews of his day ({{Romans 11:9-10|Romans 11:9–10}}).
Peter quoted this verse after the death of Judas Iscariot ({{Acts 1:20|Acts 1:20}}).
*May they be blotted out of the Book of Life*: Compare {{Psalm 1:5-6|Psalm 1:5–6}}; {{Psalm 9:5|9:5}}; {{Revelation 3:5|Revelation 3:5}}; {{Revelation 20:15|20:15}}; {{Revelation 21:22-27|21:22–27}}.
The psalmist prays that his pain will turn to praise.
Making a vow often included a sacrifice ({{Psalm 20:3|Psalms 20:3}}; {{Psalm 51:19|51:19}}; compare {{Psalm 50:13-14|50:13–14}}; {{Psalm 51:16|51:16}}).

The psalmist prays for Zion, offering a new petition from a new circumstance. He applies the prayer ({{Psalm 69:1-33|Psalm 69:1–33}}) to the desperate condition of Judah (see {{Psalm 51:18-19|51:18–19}}).
God’s people will inherit the land because the wicked will perish (see {{Psalm 37:8-9|Psalm 37:8–9}}).
*To bring remembrance*: The meaning of this phrase is not known (also found in {{Psalm 38:1|Psalm 38:1}}).

This psalm is almost exactly the same as {{Psalm 40:13-17|Psalm 40:13–17}}. It has an urgent tone ({{Psalm 70:1|Psalm 70:1}}, {{Psalm 70:5|5}}) that matches the nearby psalms (compare {{Psalm 69:17|69:17}}; {{Psalm 71:12|71:12}}).
